endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Identify and document tools and resources available and needed for standard documentation of all AI systems and for integrating them into an AI inventory, such as adopting a Model Card.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Review and maintenance of policies and procedures to account for newly encountered uses;

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Determine if the implementer organization has developed and documented an incident response plan that is updated with appropriate frequency.

endorsements.title: Developing, purchasing, implementing and monitoring AI tools in radiology: practical considerations. A multi-society statement
endorsements.issuer: ACR, CAR, ESR, RANZCR, RSNA; Radiol Artif Intell 2024 (PMID 38251899, doi:10.1148/ryai.230513)
endorsements.quote: A streamlined process to address and mitigate failures should be in place to prevent repeating mistakes.

endorsements.title: Guardrails for GenAI drafted replies in patient portal messaging
endorsements.issuer: Sakr J. npj Digital Medicine 2026;9 (PMID 41942581, doi:10.1038/s41746-026-02621-6)
endorsements.quote: A practical approach is a stable, institution-level disclosure that: - the clinician remains responsible, - AI may assist with drafting, - the message was reviewed by the clinical team, - urgent symptoms require emergency services regardless of portal response time.

commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether AI incident response plans, or rehearsing them, shorten or reduce harm during AI incidents, and no supplied study documents the hazard itself. The recommendation currently rests on five framework, guidance, and commentary endorsements, only some of which address incident response directly.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions this yields no direct evidence. The five endorsements reflect expert consensus rather than measured outcomes, and two of them (the CHAI playbook item on model cards and the portal disclosure commentary) do not speak to incident response.

Of the five sources, the CHAI Assurance Standards Guide most directly asks whether an organization has a documented incident response plan updated at appropriate frequency. NIST AI 600-1 calls for reviewing procedures as new uses arise, and the multi-society radiology statement asks for a process to address failures. None of these sources are binding regulation.

No supplied study measures how long AI-related harm persists with or without a response plan, so the size of the benefit is unknown. The radiology statement frames failure handling as a way to prevent repeated mistakes, which is a plausible mechanism that has not been tested in the supplied evidence.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that document how often AI incidents occur in health care, how long they take to detect and contain, and whether organizations with documented and rehearsed response plans achieve shorter time to containment or fewer patient harms than organizations without them. Tabletop or simulation studies comparing rehearsed and unrehearsed teams would provide a feasible first test.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Organizations serving these groups may have fewer staff to build and rehearse response plans, and whether incidents affect these patients differently remains unmeasured.
